## Introduction

Data visualization is a crucial skill in data science and analytics. In this tutorial, we will explore how to create various types of visualizations in R using the ggplot2 package, a powerful tool for creating informative and aesthetically pleasing graphics.

## Installing and Loading Required Packages

Before we begin, ensure you have the necessary packages installed. To avoid any errors, install these at minimum to ensure their most recent versions:

```{r}
install.packages(c("xfun", "knitr", "rmarkdown"))
```

Then check that these packages are here:

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggridges)
library(datasauRus)
library(colorspace)
library(pheatmap)
library(survival)
library(survminer)
library(qqman)
library(plotly)
library(ggridges)
library(gganimate)
library(gifski)
library(palmerpenguins)
library(gapminder)
```

## Module 1: Brief Review of Basic Visualization in R

Let's start with the simple built-in penguins data set to get familiar with the structure of ggplot2.

```{r}
data(penguins)
head(penguins)
penguins <- penguins %>% drop_na()

# Basic scatter plot
ggplot(penguins) +
  geom_point(aes(x = bill_length_mm, 
                 y = bill_depth_mm))
```

For this workshop, we will mostly use a "simple" [RNA-seq dataset](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE164073) on the transcriptional response to SARS-CoV-2 infection in eye tissue from human donors. 

Run this cell first to do some quick data cleanup.

```{r}
counts <- read_csv("GSE164073_Eye_count_matrix.csv.gz")   # reads .gz directly

# Some genes have zero reads in every sample - let's drop them
counts <- counts %>% filter(rowSums(across(-Gene)) > 0)

expr <- counts %>%
  pivot_longer(-Gene, names_to = "sample", values_to = "count") %>%
  separate_wider_delim(sample, delim = "_",
                       names = c("id", "tissue", "condition", "replicate"),
                       cols_remove = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(condition = factor(condition, levels = c("mock", "CoV2"))) %>%
  group_by(sample) %>%
  mutate(cpm     = count / sum(count) * 1e6,   # counts per million
         log_cpm = log2(cpm + 1)) %>%
  ungroup()

```

Now let's explore the dataset. 

```{r}
head(expr, 5) # check the first 5 rows
```

We can also create a per-sample summary table. The whole dataset is one row per gene per sample, which is a lot (tens of thousands) of rows for each sample. Here, we take the 18 distinct samples and summarize their info into one row for each. 

```{r}
samples <- expr %>%
  group_by(sample, tissue, condition, replicate) %>%
  summarise(library_size = sum(count), genes_detected = sum(count > 0), .groups = "drop")
```

We want to group by sample, but we also want to keep tissue, condition, and replicate in the output. So, we use `group_by(sample, tissue, condition, replicate)`. In `summarize`, we condense the info for each sample into `library_size` - how many reads across every gene in the sample?

We'll use both `samples` and `expr` for our visualizations depending on what we want to compare going forward. Now, let's use the dataset to build different useful plots!

### 1.1 bar plot

Bar plot is used to visually compare categorical data by representing values with rectangular bars.

```{r}
# bar plot: discrete variable
ggplot(samples, aes(x = sample, y = library_size / 1e6, fill = condition)) + 
  geom_col() + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

### 1.2 histogram/ frequency/ density plot

A histogram, frequency plot, and density plot all visualize the distribution of a dataset, but they differ in how they represent data: a histogram groups data into bins and shows counts, a frequency plot connects points representing counts for each bin, and a density plot estimates the probability density function, providing a smooth representation of distribution shape.

```{r}
# histogram plot: continuous variable
ggplot(expr, aes(x = log_cpm)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5)

# frequency plot
ggplot(expr, aes(x = log_cpm, colour = tissue)) + geom_freqpoly(binwidth = 0.5)

# density plot (smooth histogram = density plot)
ggplot(expr, aes(x = log_cpm, colour = sample)) + geom_density()
```

### 1.3 box plot

A box plot is used to summarize the distribution of a dataset by displaying its median, quartiles, and potential outliers, helping to identify variability and skewness.

```{r}
# box plot: one discrete variable + one continuous variable
ggplot(expr, aes(x = sample, y = log_cpm, fill = tissue)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

### 1.4 violin plot

A violin plot combines aspects of a box plot and a density plot to show the distribution, probability density, and variability of a dataset, making it easier to identify patterns and multimodal distributions.

```{r}
# violin plot
ggplot(expr, aes(x = tissue, y = log_cpm, fill = tissue)) + geom_violin(trim = FALSE, alpha = 0.5)
  stat_summary(
    fun = mean,
    fun.max = function(x) {
      mean(x) + sd(x)
    },
    fun.min = function(x) {
      mean(x) - sd(x)
    },
    geom = "pointrange"
  )
```

### 1.5 Example 1

Let's see an example of how to improve a data visualization plot step by step. We'll look at our RNA-seq dataset to investigate how SARS-CoV-2 infection changes the expression of one gene, **SOD2**, in three tissues of the human eye.

SOD2 (superoxide dismutase 2) is an enzyme that protects cells from oxidative stress and is commonly switched on during inflammation. It is one of the genes that changes most clearly after infection in this dataset.

#### 1.5.1 Create the dataset we will use in this example

The count matrix has one row per gene and one column per sample. To compare samples fairly, we convert counts to counts per million (CPM) (correcting for each sample's sequencing depth) and then log-transform them. We need every gene to calculate each sample's library size, but we only keep SOD2 for this example.

```{r}
# total reads per sample (library size), named by sample
lib_size <- colSums(counts[, -1])

sod2_df <- counts %>%
  filter(Gene == "SOD2") %>%
  pivot_longer(-Gene, names_to = "sample", values_to = "count") %>%
  # sample names look like "MW4_cornea_CoV2_1"
  separate_wider_delim(
    sample,
    delim = "_",
    names = c("id", "tissue", "condition", "replicate"),
    cols_remove = FALSE
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    log_cpm = log2(count / lib_size[sample] * 1e6 + 1),
    tissue = str_to_title(tissue),
    condition = fct_recode(
      factor(condition, levels = c("mock", "CoV2")),
      Mock = "mock",
      `SARS-CoV-2` = "CoV2"
    ),
    # one x-axis group per tissue x condition, in a sensible order
    group = factor(
      paste(tissue, condition, sep = "\n"),
      levels = paste(rep(c("Cornea", "Limbus", "Sclera"), each = 2),
                     c("Mock", "SARS-CoV-2"), sep = "\n")
    )
  ) %>%
  select(sample, tissue, condition, group, log_cpm)

head(sod2_df)
```

Let's also define a theme once here so that we don't have to keep repeating it for following code blocks:

```{r}
theme_example <- theme_classic(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(color = "black", size = 12),
    plot.margin = margin(3, 7, 3, 1.5)
  )

y_label <- "SOD2 expression (log2 CPM + 1)"
```

#### 1.5.2 What's the problem of the following plot?

```{r}
# points-errorbars
sod2_errbar <- sod2_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = log_cpm)) +
  stat_summary(
    fun = mean,
    fun.max = function(x) {
      mean(x) + 2 * sd(x)
    },
    fun.min = function(x) {
      mean(x) - 2 * sd(x)
    },
    geom = "pointrange"
  ) +
  xlab(NULL) +
  ylab(y_label) +
  theme_example

sod2_errbar
```

#### 1.5.3 Use box/violin plot to show the distribution

```{r}
# box plot
sod2_box <- sod2_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = log_cpm)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "grey90") +
  xlab(NULL) +
  ylab(y_label) +
  theme_example

sod2_box

# violin plot
sod2_violin <- sod2_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = log_cpm)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "grey90") +
  xlab(NULL) +
  ylab(y_label) +
  theme_example

sod2_violin
```

#### 1.5.4 Use points to show the original data

```{r}
# points
sod2_points <- sod2_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = log_cpm)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  xlab(NULL) +
  ylab(y_label) +
  theme_example

sod2_points

# jitter points
sod2_jitter <- sod2_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = log_cpm)) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(width = .15, height = 0, seed = 320),
    size = 2
  ) +
  xlab(NULL) +
  ylab(y_label) +
  theme_example

sod2_jitter
```

#### 1.5.5 Use sina plot to combine violin plot and jitter points?

What if we combine two things, and add in the data points to a violin plot to see if the points show the distribution's shape? 

```{r}
# violin + jitter
sod2_violin_jitter <- sod2_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = log_cpm)) +
  geom_violin(color = "transparent", fill = "gray90") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, size = 2) +
  xlab(NULL) +
  ylab(y_label) +
  theme_example

sod2_violin_jitter
```

With only 3 points per group, the violin plot is shapes that aren't necessarily reflecting the data. With small sample sizes, using a technique that shows the raw points is the best. Let's try something else.

#### 1.5.6 A better plot for small groups: points with a mean

Instead of a violin, we can add a short line at each group's mean and use color to separate the conditions.

```{r}
sod2_final <- sod2_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = log_cpm, color = condition)) +
  stat_summary(
    fun = mean,
    geom = "crossbar",
    width = 0.5,
    linewidth = 0.4,
    color = "grey40"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    position = position_jitter(width = .1, height = 0, seed = 320),
    size = 2.5
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Mock = "grey50", `SARS-CoV-2` = "firebrick")) +
  xlab(NULL) +
  ylab(y_label) +
  labs(
    color = NULL,
    caption = "Points are individual samples (n = 3 per group). Lines are group means."
  ) +
  theme_example +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

sod2_final
```

Compared with the earlier plot, the reader can now see every measurement, how many samples there are, and how consistent the replicates are.

## Module 2: Advanced Customization and Data Transformation

### 2.0 Prepare the dataset
Let's continue using the same RNA-seq dataset, but we'll create one more small table to use in our plotting. This one is genes by sample and each gene's variance across samples.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(colorspace)

# long format: one row per gene per sample
expr <- counts %>%
  pivot_longer(-Gene, names_to = "sample", values_to = "count") %>%
  separate_wider_delim(
    sample,
    delim = "_",
    names = c("id", "tissue", "condition", "replicate"),
    cols_remove = FALSE
  ) %>%
  mutate(condition = factor(condition, levels = c("mock", "CoV2"))) %>%
  group_by(sample) %>%
  mutate(
    cpm = count / sum(count) * 1e6,   # counts per million
    log_cpm = log2(cpm + 1)
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(group = factor(
    paste(tissue, condition),
    levels = c("cornea mock", "cornea CoV2",
               "limbus mock", "limbus CoV2",
               "sclera mock", "sclera CoV2")
  ))

# one row per sample
samples <- expr %>%
  group_by(sample, tissue, condition, replicate) %>%
  summarise(
    library_size = sum(count) / 1e6,   # millions of reads
    genes_detected = sum(count > 0),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# gene x sample matrix of log_cpm, and each gene's variance across samples
expr_mat <- expr %>%
  select(Gene, sample, log_cpm) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = sample, values_from = log_cpm) %>%
  column_to_rownames("Gene") %>%
  as.matrix()

gene_var <- apply(expr_mat, 1, var)
```

### 2.1 Data Transformations and Faceting

In data visualization, data transformation is a crucial step to ensure that the data is in the right format and structure for effective visual representation.

#### 2.1.1 Log Transformation

There are many different data transformation methods, and the following is an example of log transformation.

We would like to investigate the relationship between how highly a gene is expressed and how much it changes after SARS-CoV-2 infection, across different tissues. (This is also called an MA plot.)

```{r}
# Step 1: calculate the mean CPM of each gene in mock and infected samples, per tissue
gene_summary <- expr %>%
  group_by(tissue, Gene, condition) %>%
  summarise(mean_cpm = mean(cpm), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = condition, values_from = mean_cpm) %>%
  mutate(
    avg_cpm = (mock + CoV2) / 2,               # average expression
    log2FC = log2((CoV2 + 1) / (mock + 1))     # log2 fold change, infected vs mock
  ) %>%
  filter(avg_cpm >= 1)                         # drop barely expressed genes
gene_summary

# Step 2: draw the plot
gene_summary %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = avg_cpm, y = log2FC)) +
    geom_point(aes(color = tissue), size = 0.5, alpha = 0.3)

# Step 3: log transformation of x-axis (avg_cpm)
gene_summary %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = avg_cpm, y = log2FC)) +
    geom_point(aes(color = tissue), size = 0.5, alpha = 0.3) +
    scale_x_log10()

# Step 4 (Optional): add comma format or unit format to label the axis for better interpretation
gene_summary %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = avg_cpm, y = log2FC)) +
    geom_point(aes(color = tissue), size = 0.5, alpha = 0.3) +
    scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000),
                  labels = scales::label_comma())

gene_summary %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = avg_cpm, y = log2FC)) +
    geom_point(aes(color = tissue), size = 0.5, alpha = 0.3) +
    scale_x_log10(
      name = "Average expression",
      breaks = c(1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000),
      labels = scales::unit_format(unit = "CPM"))
```

#### 2.1.2 Faceting

Data faceting is used in data visualization to break down data into subsets and display them across multiple smaller plots. This technique helps in revealing patterns, trends, and relationships that might be obscured in a single, aggregated plot. The following is an example of data faceting.

```{r}
# facet_grid(): create a grid of graphs, by rows and columns
expr %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = log_cpm)) +
  geom_density() +
  facet_grid(. ~ tissue)

expr %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = log_cpm)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  facet_grid(tissue ~ .)

# facet_wrap(): create small multiples by "wrapping" a series of plots
gene_summary %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = avg_cpm, y = log2FC)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~tissue)
```

### 2.2 Advanced Aesthetic Customization - color

Color plays a crucial role in data visualization. We will explore how to use ColorSpace to create plots tailored to different data types.

Show all available color in colorspace.

```{r}
hcl_palettes(plot = TRUE)

hcl_palettes("qualitative", plot = TRUE)
hcl_palettes("sequential (single-hue)", n = 7, plot = TRUE)
hcl_palettes("sequential (multi-hue)", n = 7, plot = TRUE)
hcl_palettes("diverging", n = 7, plot = TRUE)
```

#### 2.2.1 qualitative colors

Qualitative (PCA of samples): principal component analysis (PCA) summarizes the expression of many genes into a few new variables (PC1, PC2, ...) that capture the biggest differences between samples. Create a scatter plot of PC1 vs. PC2, coloring points by tissue.

Qualitative (iris dataset) : create a scatter plot of Sepal.Length vs. Sepal.Width, coloring points by Species.

```{r}
# Example - RNA-seq data
# PCA on the 500 most variable genes
top500 <- names(sort(gene_var, decreasing = TRUE))[1:500]
pca <- prcomp(t(expr_mat[top500, ]))

pca_df <- as_tibble(pca$x[, 1:2], rownames = "sample") %>%
  left_join(samples, by = "sample")

# qualitative colors (Categorical Data)
ggplot(pca_df, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = tissue)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_color_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 3") +  # Using discrete qualitative color scale
  ggtitle("Qualitative Colors Example: Samples by Tissue")


# Example: built-in iris data set
ggplot(iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width, color = Species)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_color_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 3") +  # Using discrete qualitative color scale
  ggtitle("Qualitative Colors Example: Iris Species")
```

#### 2.2.2 Sequential(single-hue) colors

Sequential single-hue (samples table): create a bar plot of samples based on their library size (total reads, in millions), using a single-hue sequential color gradient.

Sequential single-hue (mtcars dataset): create a bar plot of car models (rownames(mtcars)) based on their miles per gallon (mpg), using a single-hue sequential color gradient.

```{r}
# sequential (single-hue) colors (Ordered Data - RNA-seq example)
ggplot(samples, aes(x = reorder(sample, library_size), y = library_size, fill = library_size)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  scale_fill_continuous_sequential(palette = "Blues 3") +  # Sequential color for fill
  coord_flip() + # Flip for better readability
  ylab("Library size (millions of reads)") +
  xlab("Sample") +
  ggtitle("Sequential (Single-Hue) Colors Example: Library Size per Sample") +
  theme_minimal()


# sequential (single-hue) colors (Ordered Data)
# Order data by mpg
mtcars$car <- rownames(mtcars)
mtcars <- mtcars[order(mtcars$mpg), ]
# Create a bar plot
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = reorder(car, mpg), y = mpg, fill = mpg)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  scale_fill_continuous_sequential(palette = "Blues 3") +  # Sequential color for fill
  coord_flip() + # Flip for better readability
  ggtitle("Sequential (Single-Hue) Colors Example: MPG in mtcars") +
  theme_minimal()
```

#### 2.2.3 Sequential (multi-hue) colors

Sequential multi-hue (expression heatmap): the heatmap shows the expression of the 30 most variable genes in every sample using color intensity. It highlights which genes are highly expressed in which samples.

Sequential multi-hue (volcano dataset): The volcano heatmap provides a 2D topographic view of elevation data using color intensity. It highlights how terrain elevation changes over space.

```{r}
# Example: RNA-seq dataset
# sequential (multi-hue) colors (Ordered Data)
top30 <- names(sort(gene_var, decreasing = TRUE))[1:30]

# Plot the heatmap
expr %>%
  filter(Gene %in% top30) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = sample, y = Gene, fill = log_cpm)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_continuous_sequential(palette = "YlOrRd") +  # Sequential multi-hue color scale
  ggtitle("Sequential (Multi-Hue) Colors Example: Top 30 Variable Genes") +
  xlab("Sample") +
  ylab("Gene") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

# sequential (multi-hue) colors (Ordered Data)
# Convert volcano dataset to long format for ggplot
volcano_df <- as.data.frame(as.table(volcano))
colnames(volcano_df) <- c("x", "y", "elevation")
# Plot the heatmap
ggplot(volcano_df, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = elevation)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_continuous_sequential(palette = "YlOrRd") +  # Sequential multi-hue color scale
  ggtitle("Sequential (Multi-Hue) Colors Example: Volcano Elevation") +
  xlab("X Coordinate") +  # Add x-axis label
  ylab("Y Coordinate") +  # Add y-axis label
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_blank(),   # Remove axis text
    axis.ticks = element_blank()   # Remove axis ticks
  )
```

#### 2.2.4 Diverging colors

Diverging (cornea fold changes): map the log2 fold change of the genes that changed most after infection in cornea, using a diverging color scale. The goal is to understand which genes go up and which go down after infection. A positive value means the gene is higher in infected samples, while a negative value means it is lower. Zero (no change) is a meaningful middle point.

Diverging (USArrests dataset): map UrbanPop deviation from the median across states using a diverging color scale. The goal is to understand how each state's urban population percentage compares to the median urban population percentage. A positive value means the state's urban population is above the median, while a negative value means it is below the median.

```{r}
# diverging colors (cornea fold changes)
# 30 genes with the largest change; avg_cpm >= 10 avoids noisy, barely expressed genes
cornea_fc <- gene_summary %>%
  filter(tissue == "cornea", avg_cpm >= 10) %>%
  slice_max(abs(log2FC), n = 30)

# Create a bar plot
ggplot(cornea_fc, aes(x = reorder(Gene, log2FC), y = log2FC, fill = log2FC)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  scale_fill_continuous_divergingx(palette = "RdBu", rev = TRUE) +  # rev: red = up, blue = down
  coord_flip() +
  xlab("Gene") +
  ggtitle("Diverging Colors Example: Fold Change after Infection in Cornea") +
  theme_minimal()


# diverging colors (USArrest Dataset)
# Compute deviation from median
USArrests$State <- rownames(USArrests)
USArrests$UrbanPop_dev <- USArrests$UrbanPop - median(USArrests$UrbanPop)
# Create a bar plot
ggplot(USArrests, aes(x = reorder(State, UrbanPop_dev), y = UrbanPop_dev, fill = UrbanPop_dev)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  scale_fill_continuous_divergingx(palette = "RdBu") +
  coord_flip() +
  ggtitle("Diverging Colors Example: UrbanPop Deviation in USArrests") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### 2.3 Example 2

Compare the before-and-after heatmaps below to see how color choice enhance readability and perceptual accuracy in data visualization. The heatmap shows the mean expression of several inflammation-related genes in each tissue and condition.

#### 2.3.1 Before

Use the default color to create the heatmap.

```{r}
# before
inflam_genes <- c("SOD2", "C3", "CXCL1", "CXCL6", "TNFAIP6", "CFB", "TNFAIP3")

expr %>%
  filter(Gene %in% inflam_genes) %>%
  group_by(group, Gene) %>%
  summarise(mean_log_cpm = mean(log_cpm), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = Gene, fill = mean_log_cpm)) +
  geom_tile() +
  theme_classic()
```

#### 2.3.2 After

Use the Sequential color to show the heatmap.

```{r}
# color choice 1 (Viridis)
expr %>%
  filter(Gene %in% inflam_genes) %>%
  group_by(group, Gene) %>%
  summarise(mean_log_cpm = mean(log_cpm), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = Gene, fill = mean_log_cpm)) +
  geom_tile() +
  theme_classic() +
  scale_fill_continuous_sequential(palette = "Viridis", rev = FALSE)

# color choice 2 (Inferno)
expr %>%
  filter(Gene %in% inflam_genes) %>%
  group_by(group, Gene) %>%
  summarise(mean_log_cpm = mean(log_cpm), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = group, y = Gene, fill = mean_log_cpm)) +
  geom_tile() +
  theme_classic() +
  scale_fill_continuous_sequential(palette = "Inferno", begin = 0.15, rev = FALSE)
```

### 2.4 Size & Transparency

Explore how to adjust the size and transparency of the points to enhance readability. Each point is one gene in one tissue, comparing its mean expression in mock (x) and infected (y) samples. When you have this many points (like about 40,000), size and transparency make a big difference.

```{r}
ggplot(gene_summary) +
  geom_point(aes(x = mock + 1,
                 y = CoV2 + 1,
                 color = tissue),
             size = 2,
             alpha = 0.4) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10()

ggplot(gene_summary) +
  geom_point(aes(x = mock + 1,
                 y = CoV2 + 1,
                 color = tissue),
             size = 4,
             alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10()
```

### 2.5 Legend

The legend plays a crucial role in interpreting the plot. Below, we will explore how to adjust its appearance, create different legends for different layers, and learn how to delete or merge legends effectively.

```{r}
ggplot(gene_summary, aes(x = mock + 1, y = CoV2 + 1, color = tissue)) +
  geom_point(size = 1, alpha = 0.4) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10()
```

#### 2.5.1 Adjust the appearance of the legend

```{r}
# Adjust the appearance of the legend
ggplot(gene_summary, aes(x = mock + 1, y = CoV2 + 1, color = tissue)) +
  geom_point(size = 1, alpha = 0.4) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3, alpha = 1)))
```

#### 2.5.2 Generate different legends for different layers

```{r}
# Generate different legends for different layers
ggplot(gene_summary, aes(x = mock + 1, y = CoV2 + 1, color = tissue)) +
  geom_point(size = 1, alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10()

ggplot(gene_summary, aes(x = mock + 1, y = CoV2 + 1, color = tissue)) +
  geom_point(aes(alpha = "Observed"), size = 1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, aes(alpha = "Fitted")) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_alpha_manual(
    name = NULL,
    values = c(Observed = 0.4, Fitted = 1),
    breaks = c("Observed", "Fitted")
  ) +
  guides(alpha = guide_legend(override.aes = list(
    linetype = c(0, 1),
    shape = c(16, NA),
    color = "black"
  )))
```

#### 2.5.3 Delete legend

```{r}
# delete legend
pca_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = tissue, size = library_size)) +
  geom_point()

pca_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = tissue, size = library_size)) +
  geom_point() +
  guides(
    color = guide_legend("tissue"),      # keep
    size = "none"                        # remove
  )
```

#### 2.5.4 Merge legend

```{r}
# merge legend
pca_df %>%
  ggplot(
    aes(x = PC1, y = PC2,
      color = library_size, size = library_size)
  ) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_color_viridis_c()

# method 1
pca_df %>%
  ggplot(
    aes(x = PC1, y = PC2,
      color = library_size, size = library_size)
  ) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_color_viridis_c() +
  guides(
    color = guide_legend(),
    size = guide_legend()
  )

# method 2
pca_df %>%
  ggplot(
    aes(x = PC1, y = PC2,
      color = library_size, size = library_size)
  ) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(guide = "legend")
```

### 2.6 Theme

Explore how to change the theme of the plots.

```{r}
df <- data.frame(x = 1:3, y = 1:3)
base <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) + geom_point()
# default theme
base + theme_grey() + ggtitle("theme_grey()")
# other built-in themes in ggplot2
base + theme_bw() + ggtitle("theme_bw()")
base + theme_linedraw() + ggtitle("theme_linedraw()")
base + theme_light() + ggtitle("theme_light()")
base + theme_dark() + ggtitle("theme_dark()")
base + theme_minimal()  + ggtitle("theme_minimal()")
base + theme_classic() + ggtitle("theme_classic()")
base + theme_void() + ggtitle("theme_void()")
```

### 2.7 Exercise 1

Improve the plot based on the following requirements.

1.  Improving the axes and legend labels
2.  Adding a title for the plot
3.  Tweaking the color scale to your favorite palette
4.  The background should be white, not pale grey
5.  Major gridlines should be a pale grey and minor gridlines should be removed
6.  The plot title should be centered in 12pt bold text

```{r}
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, color = species)) +
  geom_point()
```

The answer is as follows. Do not open the answer code block before completing this exercise.

```{r}
# answer
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm, color = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Penguin Bill Length vs. Depth",  # Add title
    x = "Bill Length (mm)",  # Improve x-axis label
    y = "Bill Depth (mm)",   # Improve y-axis label
    color = "Species"        # Improve legend label
  ) +
  scale_color_discrete_qualitative(palette = "Dark 3") + # Choose a favorite color palette
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +  # Set white background and base size
  theme(
    legend.justification = c(0.5, 0.5),  # Adjust legend positioning
    legend.title = element_text(size = 10),  # Set legend title font size
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),   # Set legend text font size
    plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),  # Title centered in 12pt bold
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "grey90"),  # Pale grey major gridlines
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),  # Remove minor gridlines
    panel.background = element_blank()  # Set background to white
  )

```

## Module 3. Advanced Visualization Techniques

Next, we will explore some specialized plots and learn which types of data are best suited for each. To avoid version errors, if you're using a new version of R and want to make sure, re-install these:

```{r}
install.packages("plotly")
install.packages("ggplot2")
```


Check for these libraries:

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(colorspace)
library(pheatmap)
library(plotly)
library(ggplot2)
library(gganimate)
library(gifski)
library(survival)
library(survminer)
library(qqman)
```

### 3.1 Specialized plot - heatmaps

```{r}
# base R: heatmap() function
data <- matrix(rnorm(100), nrow = 10)
rownames(data) <- paste("Row", 1:10)
colnames(data) <- paste("Col", 1:10)
heatmap(data)

# ggplot2 with geom_tile()
data <- expand.grid(Row = LETTERS[1:5], Column = LETTERS[6:10])
data$Value <- runif(nrow(data), 1, 100)
ggplot(data, aes(x = Column, y = Row, fill = Value)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_continuous_sequential(palette = "Inferno", rev = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Heatmap using ggplot2", x = "Columns", y = "Rows", fill = "Value") +
  theme_minimal()

# pheatmap for annotated heatmaps
data <- matrix(rnorm(100), nrow = 10)
rownames(data) <- paste("Gene", 1:10)
colnames(data) <- paste("Sample", 1:10)
pheatmap(data, color = colorRampPalette(c("blue", "white", "red"))(50))
```

### 3.2 Specialized plot - KM Curve

```{r}
# The 'lung' dataset is already loaded from the 'survival' library!

# Create a survival object
surv_object <- Surv(time = lung$time, event = lung$status)

# Fit a Kaplan-Meier survival curve by group
km_fit_group <- survfit(surv_object ~ sex, data = lung)

# Plot the Kaplan-Meier curves for groups
ggsurvplot(
  km_fit_group,
  data = lung,
  conf.int = TRUE,
  pval = TRUE,              # Add p-value from log-rank test
  xlab = "Time (days)",
  ylab = "Survival Probability",
  title = "Kaplan-Meier Curve by Sex",
  palette = c("blue", "red"), # Different colors for groups
  legend.labs = c("Male", "Female"), # Custom legend labels
  ggtheme = theme_minimal()
)
```

### 3.3 Specialized plot - Manhattan plot

```{r}
# Load the geuvadis dataset
data("gwasResults")

# Inspect the first few rows
head(gwasResults)

# Structure of the data
# SNP: SNP identifier
# CHR: Chromosome
# BP: Base-pair position
# P: P-value

manhattan(
  gwasResults,
  chr = "CHR",       # Chromosome column
  bp = "BP",         # Base-pair position column
  p = "P",           # P-value column
  snp = "SNP",       # SNP column
  genomewideline = -log10(5e-8),  # Genome-wide significance threshold
  suggestiveline = -log10(1e-5),  # Suggestive significance threshold
  main = "Manhattan Plot", # Title
  annotatePval = 0.01
)

```

### 3.4 Specialized plot - 2d density plot

```{r}
# Scatter plot
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Simple 2D Density Plot",
       x = "Carat",
       y = "Price")

# 2D density plot
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
  geom_bin2d(bins = 100) +
  scale_fill_continuous(type = "viridis") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Simple 2D Density Plot",
       x = "Carat",
       y = "Price")
```

### 3.5 Interactive plot - plotly

Interactive plots allow users to explore data more deeply through actions like clicking, zooming, or hovering, providing richer insights and making the data more understandable and engaging. Next, we will explore how to make plots interactive.

#### 3.5.1 ggplotly

```{r}
p <- ggplot(penguins) +
  geom_point(aes(x = bill_length_mm, 
                 y = bill_depth_mm, 
                 color = species))

ggplotly(p)
```

#### 3.5.2 Customize tooltip

What if we are interested in which island the penguin lives or any other information?

```{r, warning = FALSE}
penguins <- penguins %>%
  mutate(text = paste(
    "Island: ", island,
    "\nSpecies: ", species,
    "\nBill Length (mm): ", bill_length_mm,
    "\nBill Depth (mm): ", bill_depth_mm,
    "\nFlipper Length (mm): ",flipper_length_mm,
    "\nBody Mass (g): ", body_mass_g, sep=""
  ))
p <- ggplot(penguins) +
  geom_point(aes(x = bill_length_mm, 
                 y = bill_depth_mm, 
                 color = species,
                 text = text)) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
ggplotly(p, tooltip="text")
```

#### 3.5.3 More advanced customization

Adjust the tooltip based on the following requests.

1.  Use bold text to make the tooltip more readable

2.  Add a title to the tooltip

3.  Change the background color of the tooltip to white

4.  Change the font color of the tooltip to black

```{r, warning = FALSE}
penguins <- penguins %>%
  mutate(text = paste(
    "<span style='font-size:16px;'><b>", species, "</b></span><br>",
    "<br><b>Island:</b> ", island,
    "<br><b>Bill Length (mm):</b> ", bill_length_mm,
    "<br><b>Bill Depth (mm):</b> ", bill_depth_mm,
    "<br><b>Flipper Length (mm):</b> ",flipper_length_mm,
    "<br><b>Body Mass (g):</b> ", body_mass_g, 
    sep=""
  ))
p <- ggplot(penguins) +
  geom_point(aes(x = bill_length_mm, 
                 y = bill_depth_mm, 
                 color = species,
                 text = text)) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
pp <- ggplotly(p, tooltip="text")
pp <- pp %>%
  layout(
    hoverlabel = list(bgcolor = "white",
                      font = list(size = 12, color = "black"))
  )
pp
```

### 3.6 Animated plot - gganimate

Using gganimate to create animated plots helps visualize changes over time, making it easier to understand dynamic patterns and trends in data. It adds an extra layer of clarity by showing how variables evolve, which can be especially useful for time-series data.

```{r}
# Create the plot
plot <- ggplot(gapminder, aes(gdpPercap, lifeExp, size = pop, colour = country)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = country_colors) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 12)) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~continent) +
  # Here comes the gganimate specific bits
  labs(title = 'Year: {frame_time}', x = 'GDP per capita', y = 'life expectancy') +
  transition_time(year) +
  ease_aes('linear')

# Save at gif:
animate(plot, width = 500, height = 357, renderer = gifski_renderer())
anim_save("output.gif")
```
